title: 2 Kings 6:8–23
context: 2 Kings 6:8–23 describes Syrian raids against Israel. Elisha repeatedly warns the king of Israel where the Syrians will camp, and the king of Syria learns that the prophet knows even what he says in his bedroom. He sends a large force to seize Elisha at Dothan. Elisha’s servant is terrified, but Elisha prays and the LORD opens the young man’s eyes to see the mountain full of horses and chariots of fire. Elisha then prays for the Syrians to be struck with blindness, leads them to Samaria, and has their eyes opened there. When the king of Israel asks whether to strike them, Elisha tells him instead to feed them and send them home, and the raids stop. Both traditions read the passage as shared ground about God’s unseen protection of his servants and about mercy shown to enemies.

verses.text: Now the king of Syria was at war against Israel; and he took counsel with his servants, saying, “My camp will be in such and such a place.”
verses.arminianNotes: The king of Syria, at war with Israel, plans with his servants where to set up camp. Arminians see an enemy making careful plans, which sets up a story in which God’s knowledge overrules human strategy.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the verse introducing God’s sovereignty over the plans of nations. Both traditions read it as setting the scene for the conflict between Syrian schemes and God’s word through Elisha.

verses.text: The man of God sent to the king of Israel, saying, “Beware that you not pass this place, for the Syrians are coming down there.”
verses.arminianNotes: Elisha warns the king of Israel not to pass a certain place, because the Syrians are going down there. Arminian readers see God’s care for Israel even under an unfaithful king, with the prophet acting as a protector of the nation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and see God’s knowledge of the enemy’s plans. Both traditions read the warning as God’s mercy toward his people, given through his prophet.

verses.text: The king of Israel sent to the place which the man of God told him and warned him of; and he saved himself there, not once or twice.
verses.arminianNotes: The king of Israel sends to the place and protects himself there more than once or twice. Arminians see the king heeding the prophet’s warning and benefiting from it, which shows the value of listening to God’s word.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s protection repeated many times. Both traditions note that this king’s willingness to listen here contrasts with his anger against Elisha in 6:31.

verses.text: The king of Syria’s heart was very troubled about this. He called his servants, and said to them, “Won’t you show me which of us is for the king of Israel?”
verses.arminianNotes: The king of Syria is troubled and asks which of his servants is for the king of Israel. Arminian readers see the enemy assuming a traitor in his own camp, unable to imagine that God is revealing his plans.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and see the confusion as God frustrating human plans. Both traditions read the verse as a turning point that leads the king of Syria to target Elisha.

verses.text: One of his servants said, “No, my lord, O king; but Elisha, the prophet who is in Israel, tells the king of Israel the words that you speak in your bedroom.”
verses.arminianNotes: A servant says that Elisha tells the king of Israel even what the king of Syria says in his bedroom. Arminians see God’s knowledge reaching into the most private places, which no human secrecy can escape.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the verse as a statement of God’s complete knowledge (compare Psalm 139:1–4). Both traditions read it as showing that God’s word through his prophet exposes the plans of his enemies.

verses.text: He said, “Go and see where he is, that I may send and get him.” He was told, “Behold, he is in Dothan.”
verses.arminianNotes: The king orders them to find Elisha so he can seize him, and they report that he is in Dothan. Arminian readers see the irony of trying to capture a man who knows his enemy’s plans, which sets up God’s protection.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and see the king’s plan as futile against God’s purposes. Both traditions read the verse as moving the story toward the scene at Dothan, where God’s protection is revealed.

verses.text: Therefore he sent horses, chariots, and a great army there. They came by night and surrounded the city.
verses.arminianNotes: The king sends horses, chariots, and a great army, which surround the city by night. Arminians see an overwhelming force sent against one prophet, a picture of how hopeless the situation looks from a human point of view.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the size of the army as heightening the contrast with God’s unseen army in 6:17. Both traditions read the verse as setting up a lesson about trusting God when danger seems overwhelming.

verses.text: When the servant of the man of God had risen early and gone out, behold, an army with horses and chariots was around the city. His servant said to him, “Alas, my master! What shall we do?”
verses.arminianNotes: Elisha’s servant rises early, sees the army surrounding the city, and cries, "Alas, my master! What shall we do?" Arminian readers see understandable fear in the face of real danger, and they see the servant turning to Elisha for help.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and see the servant’s fear as the natural response when only visible realities are considered. Both traditions read the verse as preparing for the revelation of God’s protection.

verses.text: He answered, “Don’t be afraid, for those who are with us are more than those who are with them.”
verses.arminianNotes: Elisha answers, "Don’t be afraid, for those who are with us are more than those who are with them." Arminians see faith that rests on God’s presence and help rather than on what can be seen, and they see Elisha encouraging his servant.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the verse as a statement of God’s protection of his people. Both traditions treat it as shared ground and compare it with Psalm 34:7, which speaks of the LORD’s angel encamping around those who fear him.

verses.text: Elisha prayed, and said, “LORD, please open his eyes, that he may see.” the LORD opened the young man’s eyes, and he saw; and behold, the mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire around Elisha.
verses.arminianNotes: Elisha prays for the LORD to open his servant’s eyes, and he sees the mountain full of horses and chariots of fire around Elisha. Arminian readers see God answering prayer and revealing his unseen protection, which strengthens the servant’s faith.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and see the vision as showing the reality of God’s protection that is always present though unseen. Both traditions recall the chariots of fire at Elijah’s departure (2 Kings 2:11) and read the verse as shared ground about God’s care for his servants.

verses.text: When they came down to him, Elisha prayed to the LORD, and said, “Please strike this people with blindness.” He struck them with blindness according to Elisha’s word.
verses.arminianNotes: As the Syrians come down, Elisha prays for them to be struck with blindness, and the LORD does so. Arminians see God answering Elisha’s prayer in a way that disarms the enemy without bloodshed.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s power over the enemy. The word for blindness here may describe a confusion of sight rather than total blindness, and interpreters discuss its meaning. Both traditions read the verse as God protecting his servant.

verses.text: Elisha said to them, “This is not the way, neither is this the city. Follow me, and I will bring you to the man whom you seek.” He led them to Samaria.
verses.arminianNotes: Elisha tells them this is not the way or the city and leads them to Samaria, saying he will bring them to the man they seek. Arminian readers see Elisha leading the enemy into Israel’s capital, setting up an unexpected act of mercy.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree. Elisha’s words are technically true, since he does bring them to himself, and interpreters discuss how to understand them. Both traditions read the verse as part of God’s plan to end the raids through mercy rather than violence.

verses.text: When they had come into Samaria, Elisha said, “LORD, open these men’s eyes, that they may see.” The LORD opened their eyes, and they saw; and behold, they were in the middle of Samaria.
verses.arminianNotes: In Samaria Elisha prays for their eyes to be opened, and they see that they are in the middle of Samaria. Arminians see a reversal: the army that came to capture Elisha now finds itself captured.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the parallel between the servant’s eyes being opened in 6:17 and the Syrians’ eyes opened here. Both traditions read the verse as showing God’s control over what people see and understand.

verses.text: The king of Israel said to Elisha, when he saw them, “My father, shall I strike them? Shall I strike them?”
verses.arminianNotes: The king of Israel asks Elisha, "My father, shall I strike them? Shall I strike them?" Arminian readers see the king’s eagerness to take advantage of the enemy’s helplessness, and they note that he asks the prophet first.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and see the repeated question as showing his eagerness. Both traditions read the verse as setting up Elisha’s surprising command to show mercy.

verses.text: He answered, “You shall not strike them. Would you strike those whom you have taken captive with your sword and with your bow? Set bread and water before them, that they may eat and drink, then go to their master.”
verses.arminianNotes: Elisha forbids it and tells the king to set bread and water before them and send them home. Arminians see mercy toward defenseless enemies as reflecting God’s own character, and many compare it with Romans 12:20.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the command as a powerful example of mercy shown to enemies. Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about God’s mercy, which overcomes evil with good.

verses.text: He prepared a great feast for them. After they ate and drank, he sent them away and they went to their master. So the bands of Syria stopped raiding the land of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: The king prepares a great feast and sends them home, and the Syrian bands stop raiding Israel. Arminian readers see mercy bringing peace that military force had not achieved, at least for a time.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and note that the peace is temporary, since the siege begins in the next verse. Both traditions read the verse as showing the practical fruit of mercy and God’s protection of his people.
